title: В Киеве поврежден Северный мост. Его перекрыли в обе стороны
content_c:
Кроме того, чрезвычайно сложная ситуация с электроэнергией.
Во время обстрела Киева 7 ноября россияне повредили Северный мост, сообщил мэр города Виталий Кличко. Он также заявил, что число пострадавших возросло до пяти человек.
«В результате атаки врага поврежден Северный мост. Специалисты изучают степень повреждений. Движение по мосту пока закрыто в обе стороны», — сообщил Кличко.
Он добавил, что ночью враг также повредил энергообъекты в Киевской и Житомирской областях, поэтому ситуация со светом в столице чрезвычайно сложная. Соответственно, работа систем тепло- и водоснабжения также затруднена.
«Пять человек пострадали в столице в результате атаки врага. В частности, 14-летний ребенок. Двоих раненых медики госпитализировали», — добавил Кличко.
Враг атаковал Киев баллистическими ракетами в несколько волн. Также сообщалось, что, кроме столицы, россияне атаковали ракетами пригороды. Кроме того, Киевская область этой ночью подверглась атаке дронов. В частности, в селе Богдановка Броварского района вражеский дрон поразил частный дом, что привело к разрушениям и пожару. title: В Україну йдуть морози та сніг. Зеленський залучає поліцію на допомогу енергетикам Києва
content_c:
В Україну йдуть морози та сніг. Зеленський залучає поліцію на допомогу енергетикам Києва
  - Author, Відділ новин
  - Role, BBC News Україна
- Published
- Час прочитання: 3 хв
На Україну насуваються морози та перший сніг. Хоча похолодання на початку листопада - це звичне явище, але для мешканців українських міст, які залишаються без світла та води на багато годин, ситуація може суттєво погіршитися. Тим часом президент Володимир Зеленський заявив про залучення поліції до розв'язання проблем з тривалими відключеннями світла. Він втрутився в ситуацію, коли через тривалу відсутність світла кияни почали перекривати дороги.
Як повідомив Гідрометцентр, уже найближчої ночі в більшості регіонів температура опуститься до нуля, а місцями - до 3 градусів морозу.
Найхолодніше буде на заході країни, де стовпчики термометрів можуть показати до –6°. Удень 7 листопада температура становитиме лише +0…+6°.
За прогнозом синоптиків, погода буде хмарною з проясненнями.
У центральних, південних та східних регіонах вдень 6 листопада очікують мокрий сніг, на півдні та сході - з дощем, уночі та вранці можлива ожеледиця.
Таку погоду прогнозують і на наступні кілька днів, після цього буде невелике потепління.
У Києві 6 листопада прогнозують дощ, місцями з мокрим снігом. Уночі температура буде близькою до нуля, на околицях можливі невеликі морози, а вдень повітря прогріється лише до +5 °C.
Дискомфорту додаватиме північний вітер, який буде поривчастим, місцями сильним, повідомила синоптикиня Наталка Діденко.
Що з водою і світлом у Києві
Після російських обстрілів енергетичної інфраструктури в Україні залишається складна ситуація з електропостачанням.
Найгірше становище - в Києві, Житомирі та низці інших міст.
"Київ функціонує в надзвичайно складних умовах", - заявив напередодні мер міста Віталій Кличко.
У п'ятницю в столиці та області запроваджені аварійні відключення електроенергії, повідомила приватна енергетична компанія ДТЕК.
Залежно від району й конкретної адреси світла може не бути по 12-16 годин на добу.
Вдень електропостачання часто відновлюють лише на короткі проміжки - приблизно на 2-2,5 години. Між ними мешканці переживають тривалі періоди знеструмлення, які можуть сягати семи годин.
Причина цього - зупинка пошкодження не працюють три міські ТЕЦ, а електротранспорт у столиці зупинився.
Через російські атаки вночі та сьогодні вранці зʼявилися нові знеструмлення в семи областях України. Крім Київської, це також Вінницька, Дніпропетровська, Житомирська, Запорізька, Харківська ті Чернігівська, повідомляє Укренерго.
Там, де дозволяють безпекові умови, електрики ремонтують мережу, повідомили в компанії.
Через тривалі відключення електрики у Києві також стаються регулярні перебої з водопостачанням.
3 листопада через знеструмлення основних об'єктів водоканалу вода зникла в усіх районах столиці. Постачання вдалося відновити, однак 5 листопада перебої повторилися.
Вранці в пʼятницю мерія столиці повідомила, що всі водопровідні та каналізаційні насосні станції в Києві працюють у штатному режимі.
Фахівці "Київводоканалу" продовжують контролювати роботу систем водопостачання та водовідведення столиці.
Водночас міська влада визнає, що більшість об'єктів водопостачання столиці не можуть повноцінно працювати лише на звичайних генераторах, тому місто створює для них окрему систему резервного електроживлення.
Президент залучає поліцію
Тим часом Володимир Зеленський вирішив залучити поліцію до допомоги енергетикам у Києві.
4 листопада під час наради щодо ситуації в енергетиці президент заявив, що доручив уряду та правоохоронним органам підготувати план повноцінної співпраці з енергетичними компаніями, які, за його словами, відстають із ремонтами та відновленням інфраструктури.
5 листопада в інтерв'ю ТСН президент навів конкретний приклад залучення поліції.
Він розповів, що після протесту киян через тривалу відсутність світла зателефонував міністру внутрішніх справ.
Той повідомив, що поліцейські допомогли привести електриків на енергооб'єкт, де бракувало працівників.
"Дійсно на енергетичному об'єкті не було достатньо працівників. Тобто не можна ремонтувати в розвалочку, як то кажуть. І молодці, поліцейські спрацювали, привели на об'єкт електриків, все запрацювало", - сказав Зеленський.
Увечері 4 листопада в кількох районах Києва пройшли стихійні протести через тривалу відсутність електрики.
Мешканці Оболоні та району Академмістечка вийшли на дороги й тимчасово обмежили рух транспорту, вимагаючи уваги до проблеми. Зокрема, жителі будинку на вулиці Йорданській заявляли, що майже п'ять діб не мали стабільного електропостачання, а світло з'являлося лише приблизно на 20 хвилин.
Поліція Києва повідомила, що після розмови з учасниками рух транспорту вдалося відновити. На місце також направили представників ДТЕК.

title: Окупанти атакували Павлоград, пошкоджена багатоповерхівка, троє постраждалих
content_c:
Троє людей, у тому числі дитина, постраждали унаслідок російської атаки в місті Павлоград Дніпропетровської області в ніч на суботу, пошкоджений багатоповерховий житловий будинок, повідомив начальник Дніпропетровської обласної військової адміністрації (ОВА) Олександр Ганжа.
"Постраждали троє людей. 32-річний чоловік госпіталізований у стані середньої тяжкості. 38-річна жінка та 11-річна дівчинка лікуватимуться амбулаторно", – написав Ганжа в Телеграм.
За його словами, ворог ударив по місту безпілотниками. Зайнялося кілька пожеж. Пошкоджений п'ятиповерховий будинок, підприємство, автівки, господарчі споруди.
Ганжа повідомив, що загалом Дніпропетровська область пережила майже 20 дронових атак по чотирьох районах, але в решті трьох без постраждалих. title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
content_c:
Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
- Published
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.
1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentum
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.
California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.
Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
- Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff 
  - Published9 hours ago
- What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress 
  - Published2 days ago
2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for future
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.
"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."
Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
- Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide 
  - Published13 hours ago
4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earned
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.
Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.
Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
content_c:
Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.
Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.
Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."
Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.
In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time.
His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.
The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.
It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.
Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.
At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".
Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".
The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.
"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."
The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."
Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.
Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".
Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand.
On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims.
"As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."
Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.
During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

title: How does it affect me if share prices fall?
content_c:
How does it affect me if share prices fall?
- Published
Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.
The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.
As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.
Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.
Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.
Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.
'I don't invest' - actually, you probably do
Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.
Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.
Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.
Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.
So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.
Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.
Is my specific pension affected?
Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.
Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.
In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.
What happens if I'm just about to retire?
Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.
As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.
Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.
That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.
However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.
Is my job at risk?
If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.
That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.
When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.
There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.
Are stock market falls always bad?
In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).
However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.
Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.
Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.
So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.
Can anyone invest their money?
Yes, and millions of people do, but experts stress that a long-term strategy is required to ride out short-term falls. It is also important to ensure cash savings are held too, so unexpected expenses - like the need for a replacement boiler - can be covered.
The government is keen to get people in the UK to invest more, partly because it says that will help UK economic growth and partly because it is much more popular among individuals in the US and some parts of Europe.
It backed an advertising campaign to encourage people to invest, funded by some of the UK's biggest financial services firms.
But the choice of "Savvy the Squirrel" to front the campaign has raised some eyebrows. Some question whether the push could get anywhere close to the success of the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s, which encouraged people to invest in the newly privatised British Gas.
Will things get more expensive?
When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.
As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.
Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.
As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.
Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.
That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.
However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.
Is my job at risk?
If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.
That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.
When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.
There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.
Are stock market falls always bad?
In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).
However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.
Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.
Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.
So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.
Can anyone invest their money?
Yes, and millions of people do, but experts stress that a long-term strategy is required to ride out short-term falls. It is also important to ensure cash savings are held too, so unexpected expenses - like the need for a replacement boiler - can be covered.
The government is keen to get people in the UK to invest more, partly because it says that will help UK economic growth and partly because it is much more popular among individuals in the US and some parts of Europe.
It backed an advertising campaign to encourage people to invest, funded by some of the UK's biggest financial services firms.
But the choice of "Savvy the Squirrel" to front the campaign has raised some eyebrows. Some question whether the push could get anywhere close to the success of the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s, which encouraged people to invest in the newly privatised British Gas.
Will things get more expensive?
When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.
As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.
Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.
Get in touch
Are you concerned about the impact of tariffs on your business or personal finances? Do you have any questions regarding tariffs?

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
content_c:
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

title: UK government to extend controversial Palantir NHS contract as it draws up plan for British alternative – as it happened
content_c:
Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported.
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.
The system aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. But a review has concluded that removing Palantir from NHS data systems by triggering a break clause in its contract would be too disruptive, the FT reported.
Ministers instead plan to launch a procurement process for a UK tech alternative, with Palantir to potentially be replaced in two years.
Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”.
The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.
The plan is expected to be signed off soon but Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of “betrayal” and said it was “allowing the corporate capture of our most beloved institution by a genocide and Donald Trump supporting tech corporation.”
He added:
The reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.
Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.
That’s all from me, Tom Ambrose, and indeed the UK politics live blog for today.
Here is a round-up of the day’s main stories:
Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported. Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.
Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in the government’s latest “small fix” to help improve people’s lives. The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.
Andy Burnham has praised the victims who have come forward to speak about Russell Brand’s crimes, after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault against three women. Police have urged anyone with fresh allegations against Brand to come forward, with the head of Scotland Yard, Mark Rowley, saying he would not be surprised if “many more” alleged victims emerged following the former comedian and online influencer’s conviction on Thursday.
Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering a change to knife laws, following the murder of Henry Nowak. The home secretary said she had not “taken any options off the table”, after Nowak’s father, Mark Nowak, called for a clearer definition in law of what a Sikh kirpan looks like.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay. David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.
Andy Burnham has joked that he was a bad driver after getting a quiz for primary-age children about braking distance wrong. During a visit to Siemens Rail Technology Centre in Chippenham on Friday, the prime minister was invited to take part in a lesson hosted by TV presenter Maddie Moate with year five and six pupils from the town.
The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month. At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts. Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said. Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
A Scottish government official warned there were “clearly significant impacts and risks” from plans to site a number of hyperscale data centres in Scotland, documents released under freedom of information (FoI) laws have revealed. The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.
Staff at the Scottish government and four of its agencies are being balloted on potential strike action in a row over a mandatory level of office working.
The government has mandated that staff should work from one of their offices 40% of the time, which the PCS union – which represents civil servants – said is “unacceptable”.
The union is calling on the government to scrap the plan, with a ballot on potential industrial action opening on Monday and lasting until 14 December, PA reports.
Burnham says Brand’s crimes are 'horrifying' as he praises victims’ courage
Andy Burnham has praised the victims who have come forward to speak about Russell Brand’s crimes, after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault against three women.
Speaking to Times Radio, the prime minister said: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done.
“I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out. But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand and worse.
“So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to stand forward.”
‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks
Chris Osuh
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.
David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.
In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.
Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.
Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.
A Scottish government official warned there were “clearly significant impacts and risks” from plans to site a number of hyperscale data centres in Scotland, documents released under freedom of information (FoI) laws have revealed.
The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.
The official, whose name was redacted in the documents that were released, said that depending on the location of data centres “there is a clear risk here that locals bear the brunt of increased electricity prices – or even a shortage of energy, or unreliable power – while seeing little direct benefit from ‘hosting’ the data centre”.
In the document, which dates back to March, they added that to mitigate against this “there needs to be a really clear system for protecting locals from increased energy prices and power shortages, as part of a deal to host the centre”.
Andy Burnham has joked that he was a bad driver after getting a quiz for primary-age children about braking distance wrong.
During a visit to Siemens Rail Technology Centre in Chippenham on Friday, the prime minister was invited to take part in a lesson hosted by TV presenter Maddie Moate with year five and six pupils from the town.
The host asked Burnham and the children a series of questions about the braking distance of moving vehicles, with the prime minister making light of his incorrect answers.
“That shows why I’m a bad driver, doesn’t it,” he joked.
He visited the manufacturing company in Wiltshire to highlight his plans to create more work experience opportunities for young people and tackle barriers to employment.
The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.
At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.
European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.
Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.
But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns
Nadeem Badshah
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
Kaur said:
The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.
The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.
Kaur added:
Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.
Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party, who held Wednesday’s debate, said:
Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.
To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.
Minister tells energy suppliers to do more to help households tackle unpaid bills this winter
Jillian Ambrose
An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.
Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.
The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.
The minister for energy consumers, Polly Billington, is understood to have told bosses from energy companies including Octopus Energy, British Gas and EDF Energy that suppliers would still need to play a “crucial role” in tackling the longstanding issue of problem debt alongside the government’s multibillion-pound support package.
Suppliers are expected to proactively identify customers who may be under financial strain and offer help such as debt payment plans or pointing them in the direction of debt advice services.
The government is also planning to work with the industry to make it easier to spot households that may need extra help, and to modernise payment systems to make it easier to pay. The government has backed the use of smart meters and smart pre-pay meters to help households track their spending and avoid getting into arrears.
Knife law changes not 'off the table', home secretary says
Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering a change to knife laws, following the murder of Henry Nowak.
The Home Secretary said she had not “taken any options off the table”, after Nowak’s father, Mark Nowak, called for a clearer definition in law of what a Sikh kirpan looks like.
Mark Nowak told ITV News: “I fully understand the need to carry a kirpan but surely that should be defined in law, in terms of size and type and whether it should be visible, and so on and so forth.
“And therefore, anything else should be made illegal.”
Asked about Mark Nowak’s suggestion, Mahmood told the same broadcaster:
I haven’t taken any options off the table. I’m also not going in with a fixed mind about what the right clarifications of the law might be.
It’s important to get the right balance between religious expression in this country, which is something that many of us of a faith, including myself, hold very dearly, but do so in a way that is within what we expect of our citizens for the purposes of the criminal law.
Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch said lawmakers “do need to look at” knife laws.
Burnham to force employers to publish salaries on job ads in latest government 'small fix'
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in the government’s latest “small fix” to help improve people’s lives.
The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.
Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.
The prime minister said:
Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it.
That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.
But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”
Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.
Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to give lower pay offers to some candidates, including women.

A Scottish government official warned there were “clearly significant impacts and risks” from plans to site a number of hyperscale data centres in Scotland, documents released under freedom of information (FoI) laws have revealed. The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.
Staff at the Scottish government and four of its agencies are being balloted on potential strike action in a row over a mandatory level of office working.
The government has mandated that staff should work from one of their offices 40% of the time, which the PCS union – which represents civil servants – said is “unacceptable”.
The union is calling on the government to scrap the plan, with a ballot on potential industrial action opening on Monday and lasting until 14 December, PA reports.
Burnham says Brand’s crimes are 'horrifying' as he praises victims’ courage
Andy Burnham has praised the victims who have come forward to speak about Russell Brand’s crimes, after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault against three women.
Speaking to Times Radio, the prime minister said: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done.
“I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out. But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand and worse.
“So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to stand forward.”
‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks
Chris Osuh
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.
David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.
In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.
Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.
Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.
A Scottish government official warned there were “clearly significant impacts and risks” from plans to site a number of hyperscale data centres in Scotland, documents released under freedom of information (FoI) laws have revealed.
The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.
The official, whose name was redacted in the documents that were released, said that depending on the location of data centres “there is a clear risk here that locals bear the brunt of increased electricity prices – or even a shortage of energy, or unreliable power – while seeing little direct benefit from ‘hosting’ the data centre”.
In the document, which dates back to March, they added that to mitigate against this “there needs to be a really clear system for protecting locals from increased energy prices and power shortages, as part of a deal to host the centre”.
Andy Burnham has joked that he was a bad driver after getting a quiz for primary-age children about braking distance wrong.
During a visit to Siemens Rail Technology Centre in Chippenham on Friday, the prime minister was invited to take part in a lesson hosted by TV presenter Maddie Moate with year five and six pupils from the town.
The host asked Burnham and the children a series of questions about the braking distance of moving vehicles, with the prime minister making light of his incorrect answers.
“That shows why I’m a bad driver, doesn’t it,” he joked.
He visited the manufacturing company in Wiltshire to highlight his plans to create more work experience opportunities for young people and tackle barriers to employment.
The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.
At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.
European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.
Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.
But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.
Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported.
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.
The system aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. But a review has concluded that removing Palantir from NHS data systems by triggering a break clause in its contract would be too disruptive, the FT reported.
Ministers instead plan to launch a procurement process for a UK tech alternative, with Palantir to potentially be replaced in two years.
Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”.
The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.
The plan is expected to be signed off soon but Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of “betrayal” and said it was “allowing the corporate capture of our most beloved institution by a genocide and Donald Trump supporting tech corporation.”
He added:
The reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.
Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.
UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns
Nadeem Badshah
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
Kaur said:
The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.
The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.
Kaur added:
Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.
Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party, who held Wednesday’s debate, said:
Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.
To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.
Minister tells energy suppliers to do more to help households tackle unpaid bills this winter
Jillian Ambrose
An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.
Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.
The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.
The minister for energy consumers, Polly Billington, is understood to have told bosses from energy companies including Octopus Energy, British Gas and EDF Energy that suppliers would still need to play a “crucial role” in tackling the longstanding issue of problem debt alongside the government’s multibillion-pound support package.
Suppliers are expected to proactively identify customers who may be under financial strain and offer help such as debt payment plans or pointing them in the direction of debt advice services.
The government is also planning to work with the industry to make it easier to spot households that may need extra help, and to modernise payment systems to make it easier to pay. The government has backed the use of smart meters and smart pre-pay meters to help households track their spending and avoid getting into arrears.
Knife law changes not 'off the table', home secretary says
Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering a change to knife laws, following the murder of Henry Nowak.
The Home Secretary said she had not “taken any options off the table”, after Nowak’s father, Mark Nowak, called for a clearer definition in law of what a Sikh kirpan looks like.
Mark Nowak told ITV News: “I fully understand the need to carry a kirpan but surely that should be defined in law, in terms of size and type and whether it should be visible, and so on and so forth.
“And therefore, anything else should be made illegal.”
Asked about Mark Nowak’s suggestion, Mahmood told the same broadcaster:
I haven’t taken any options off the table. I’m also not going in with a fixed mind about what the right clarifications of the law might be.
It’s important to get the right balance between religious expression in this country, which is something that many of us of a faith, including myself, hold very dearly, but do so in a way that is within what we expect of our citizens for the purposes of the criminal law.
Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch said lawmakers “do need to look at” knife laws.
Burnham to force employers to publish salaries on job ads in latest government 'small fix'
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in the government’s latest “small fix” to help improve people’s lives.
The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.
Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.
The prime minister said:
Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it.
That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.
But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”
Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.
Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to give lower pay offers to some candidates, including women.

title: Cornell faculty declares 'no confidence' in university leadership
content_c:
Cornell faculty declares 'no confidence' in university leadership
November 7, 2026
Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution on Friday declaring "no confidence" in the administration's ability to handle what it has called a sexual assault crisis on campus.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.
What's behind the resolution?
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
The university leadership has faced intense criticism since mid-September when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved.
After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.
The allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was later met with widespread criticism.
The investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.
What did the board chair say about the faculty vote?
Some faculty members have criticized University President Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
The faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders but the resolution's backers had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.
After the faculty vote, Cornell Board Chair Anne Smalling said it "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable."
But she also expressed the board of trustees' support for President Kotlikoff and the administration.
"We support President Kotlikoff's commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again."
Resolution 'only the beginning'
Kotlikoff has yet to respond to the outcome of the faculty vote.
Under university procedures, the president has 30 days to respond in writing, a university spokesperson said.
Kotlikoff said the day before voting began on October 29 that faculty discussion and debate were "an important component of Cornell's shared governance."
He also pointed out that the university had taken measures including adding staff to its civil rights office, expanding sexual assault prevention education, and hiring staff focused on victim advocacy.
Iris Packman, a co-sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, told the Associated Press on Friday that the vote was "only the beginning" and that faculty would push for sweeping reforms.
Yasmeen Masoud, a Cornell junior who spoke Friday at a news conference organized by the resolution's sponsors, called the vote encouraging for students frustrated with the university's response.
"We should not have to beg for answers, demand basic transparency or generate media attention just to get our concerns acknowledged," she said. "It reminds us that there are people across this university who care deeply about its future and are willing to stand together to demand a better Cornell."
description: The university leadership has faced intense criticism for its handling of sexual crimes on campus since a former student filed a lawsuit saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.

title: Ardern führte Neuseeland durch Krisen, jetzt lehrt sie Führung
content_c:
Karriere nach der Politik Ardern führte Neuseeland durch Krisen, jetzt lehrt sie Führung
In Neuseeland wird ein neues Parlament gewählt – und eine der bekanntesten Persönlichkeiten des Landes verfolgt die Entwicklung inzwischen von der anderen Seite der Tasmansee: Jacinda Ardern (46), die das Land von 2017 bis 2023 regierte, lebt mittlerweile in Australien und hat dort vor kurzem eine neue berufliche Heimat gefunden: an der Universität Sydney.
Als Regierungschefin führte sie Neuseeland durch eine Pandemie, wurde nach dem verheerenden Terroranschlag von Christchurch weltweit für ihren empathischen Umgang mit den Opfern bewundert und galt lange als Hoffnungsträgerin einer anderen politischen Kultur. Drei Jahre nach ihrem überraschenden Rücktritt Anfang 2023 ist ihr Terminkalender auch weiter gut gefüllt.
Erst Harvard, dann die Memoiren
Schon kurz nach ihrem Abschied aus der Politik hatte es sie ins Ausland gezogen: Im Herbst 2023 übernahm sie zwei Gaststipendien an der renommierten Harvard University in den USA. Dort beschäftigte sie sich unter anderem mit Fragen politischer Führung, digitaler Verantwortung und dem Umgang mit extremistischen Inhalten im Internet.
2025 meldete sie sich als Autorin zurück: Unter dem Titel »A Different Kind of Power« veröffentlichte sie ihre Memoiren, die auch auf Deutsch erschienen sind. Darin blickt sie auf ihren ungewöhnlichen politischen Aufstieg, die großen Krisen ihrer Amtszeit und ihre Entscheidung zurück, mit nur 42 Jahren aufzuhören.
Auch in einem Dokumentarfilm mit dem schlichten Titel »Prime Minister«, der 2025 beim Sundance Film Festival Premiere feierte, gewährte sie persönliche Einblicke in ihr Leben zwischen Staatsgeschäften, Mutterschaft und wachsendem öffentlichem Druck.
Professorin an der Universität Sydney
Inzwischen hat Ardern mit ihrem Mann Clarke Gayford und Tochter Neve ihren Lebensmittelpunkt nach Australien verlegt. Seit Oktober 2026 ist sie Professorin für politische Praxis an der University of Sydney. In der Position will sie mit Studierenden und Forschern über empathische Führung, gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt, Vertrauen in die Politik und globale Gesundheitsfragen diskutieren.
Daneben engagiert sich Ardern weiterhin für den Klimaschutz, ist Mitglied des Kuratoriums von Prinz Williams Earthshot Prize und hat 2024 ein eigenes Förderprogramm für Führungspersönlichkeiten gegründet.
description: Sie machte als ebenso junge wie empathische Regierungschefin von Neuseeland weltweit Schlagzeilen. Dann trat Jacinda Ardern 2023 überraschend ab, um sich ihrer Familie zu widmen. Nun schaut sie mit Abstand auf ihre Heimat.

title: Trumps neuer Stabschef Miller: "Ein Warnschuss in Richtung des künftigen Kongresses"
content_c:
Trumps neuer Stabschef Miller "Ein Warnschuss in Richtung des künftigen Kongresses"
Auf Stabschefin Wiles folgt Hardliner Miller: Mit dieser Entscheidung reagiert Trump auf das Wahldebakel seiner Partei - und geht auf Konfrontationskurs zu den Demokraten. Doch auch Republikanern stößt die Personalie auf.
Er habe einfach einen Wechsel gewollt, sagte US-Präsident Donald Trump kurz angebunden zu Reportern. Medien berichten, Susie Wiles - die erste Frau im Amt des Stabschefs des Weißen Hauses - habe zu den Mitarbeitern gehört, die Trump für das Wahldebakel seiner Partei verantwortlich mache.
Wiles' Nachfolger Stephen Miller war bisher ihr Vize und Berater des Präsidenten für die innere Sicherheit. Er ist ein rechter Hardliner, arbeitet seit mehr als zehn Jahren für Trump und gilt als außergewöhnlich loyal. Dass der Präsident ihn auswählte, bedeutet aus Sicht des Publizisten Chris Whipple: Trump will keine Zusammenarbeit mit der künftigen demokratischen Mehrheit im Kongress.
Whipple hat ein Buch über Stabschefs geschrieben. "Die Ernennung von Miller ist ein echter Warnschuss in Richtung des künftigen Kongresses", sagt er bei CNN. "Es kommt fast einer Kriegserklärung durch Trump gleich. Miller entspricht bei weitem nicht dem Bild eines Politikers, der über das nötige politische Geschick verfügt, um mit der Opposition umzugehen. Er kennt eigentlich nur einen Gang, und das ist Vollgas in Richtung Abgrund."
"Keine weise Personalentscheidung"
Die Demokraten verstanden das Signal sofort. "Das zeigt, dass Trump nicht verstanden hat, was am Wahltag passiert ist: eine Ablehnung auf ganzer Linie von Trump, seiner MAGA-Bewegung und ihrer Politik", so der Abgeordnete Adam Smith. "Dass Trump nun noch einen draufsetzt - mit einem seiner kämpferischsten und polarisierendsten Befürworter einiger seiner extremsten politischen Maßnahmen - zeigt, dass er im Grunde nichts aus der Wahl gelernt hat und nicht erkannt hat, wo die Wählerschaft stand."
Stephen Miller gestaltet Trumps Einwanderungspolitik und lenkt ihre Umsetzung. Kritiker halten sie für brutal, grausam und völlig überzogen.
Der republikanische Abgeordnete Don Bacon sagt bei ABC, Millers Migrationskurs sei für die Wahlniederlage der Republikaner mitverantwortlich: "Menschen abzuschieben, die die meisten Amerikaner nicht abschieben wollen, war in Texas, Arizona und manchen Gegenden von Florida ein wichtiger Grund für die Niederlage", so Bacon. "Und dahinter steckte Stephen Miller. Also: keine weise Personalentscheidung."
Der Glaube an Stärke, Gewalt und Macht
Extrem sind auch Millers außenpolitische Ansichten. Im Januar legte er in einem CNN-Interview dar, dass Grönland den USA zustehe - und dass er nicht an eine regelbasierte Weltordnung glaube. "Wir leben in einer Welt, in der man zwar viel über internationale Höflichkeiten reden kann, aber die reale Welt wird von Stärke, Gewalt und Macht bestimmt", so Miller damals. "Das sind die eisernen Gesetze der Welt seit Anbeginn der Zeit."
Senator Thom Tillis, ein Republikaner, hält Trumps Personalentscheidung für "die schlechteste aller möglichen Entscheidungen":
                
                
                Wir sprechen hier davon, eine der parteiischsten und polarisierendsten Persönlichkeiten - selbst unter Republikanern - zu berufen. Wie können wir nur glauben, dass jemand mit einem so spaltenden Hintergrund wie Stephen Miller der 'Olivenzweig' sein könnte, den wir brauchen, um mit den neuen demokratischen Mehrheiten im Kongress etwas zu erreichen?
Mit den Demokraten zusammenarbeiten - oder "Mister Veto" zu sein: Wie es scheint, hat Trump sich entschieden.
